title: Psalm 118: The Stone the Builders Rejected
summary: The last psalm of the Egyptian Hallel begins and ends with the call to give thanks for the LORD's enduring love. In between, a leader who was surrounded by enemies and pushed to the edge of death tells how the LORD rescued him, then approaches the temple gates in procession. The rejected stone becomes the cornerstone, the people cry for salvation, and those at the temple bless the one who comes in the name of the LORD.
story: Psalm 118 closes the Egyptian Hallel (113 to 118) and completes its movement from the exodus of Psalm 114 to a festival of thanksgiving in the temple. It is the psalm Jewish pilgrims would have sung as they approached Jerusalem and its courts, and it was one of the songs on the lips of the crowds when Jesus entered Jerusalem. For the returned exiles it spoke of a people pushed nearly to death and brought back to worship. For the New Testament writers, it became a key text for the rejection and exaltation of Jesus.
historical:
The psalm has no heading. The speaker in verses 5 to 21 is a single person who was surrounded by nations and then rescued, and many scholars think this was originally a king returning from battle to give thanks at the temple, with the people and priests responding. Others see the speaker as representing the whole community, especially after the exile, when Israel was surrounded by hostile neighbors (compare Nehemiah 4 and 6). The psalm's date is uncertain for that reason; a royal setting would place it during the monarchy, while a communal reading fits the post-exilic period.

The psalm became closely associated with the Feast of Tabernacles (Booths), the autumn harvest festival. The Mishnah describes priests circling the altar at that feast while chanting the words of verse 25, and the waving of branches at the festival may lie behind the crowd's behavior when Jesus entered Jerusalem. Verse 14 quotes almost exactly the Song of the Sea sung after the exodus (Exodus 15:2), tying this later deliverance to the first.
cultural:
The psalm reflects a temple procession. The gates of righteousness in verse 19 are the gates of the temple, which only the righteous may enter; Psalms 15 and 24 describe similar entrance liturgies, with questions asked and answered at the gate. Verse 26 records a priestly blessing from the house of the LORD on the one who arrives. The festal sacrifice of verse 27 is the animal offered at the feast; the Hebrew is difficult, and some translations instead picture a festal procession with branches reaching to the horns of the altar, the projecting corners of the altar of sacrifice.

The cornerstone of verse 22 comes from building practice. Ancient builders chose stones carefully, and a stone could be set aside as unfit. The head of the corner has been understood either as the foundation stone that set the angle of the walls or as a capstone crowning the structure; either way it is the most important stone in the building. The prayer “O LORD, save us” in verse 25 is, in Hebrew, hoshia na, the source of the word hosanna.
literary: The psalm is framed by the same verse at the beginning and end: “Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever.” Verses 1 to 4 call Israel, the house of Aaron, and those who fear the LORD to repeat the refrain, a liturgical pattern shared with Psalm 115. Verses 5 to 18 are the speaker's testimony, full of repetition: the LORD is on my side twice, better to take refuge in the LORD twice, they surrounded me three times, in the name of the LORD I cut them off three times, the right hand of the LORD three times. Verses 19 to 28 move to the gates and into the temple, with changing voices (the speaker, the gatekeepers, the congregation, and the priests), and verse 29 closes the frame. The effect is of a drama performed in worship.

outline.t: Better to trust the LORD than people or princes
Surrounded by nations, rescued in the LORD's name
Shouts of victory: I will not die but live
The rejected stone becomes the cornerstone
Hosanna and blessing on the one who comes
You are my God; give thanks

doctrines.note: The word salvation runs through the psalm (verses 14, 15, 21, and the prayer of verse 25). God saves the speaker from death and enemies, and the people ask him to save again. Rescue is the LORD's doing, and it is “marvelous in our eyes.”
The rejected stone made cornerstone and the one who comes in the name of the LORD are applied in the New Testament to Jesus, who was rejected by Israel's leaders and exalted by God.
“It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in man.” The psalm contrasts trust in God with trust in human power, even the power of princes, and shows it tested under real threat.

words.note: Pinnah, corner. With rosh (head) it forms the phrase head of the corner, the most important stone in a building. Whether it means the foundation cornerstone or the capstone is debated, but the point is the reversal: the stone the builders discarded now holds the whole building together.

Yasha, to save, the root of the word salvation and of the names Joshua and Jesus. In verse 25 its imperative form joined to na (please) gives hoshia na, which passed into Greek and English as hosanna. Originally a plea, save us, it became a shout of praise.

Mul, a verb that normally means to circumcise. In verses 10 to 12 it is used of the speaker's defeat of the nations, rendered “I cut them off.” The unusual word has puzzled translators; some take it in the sense of cutting down, others as fending off.

Chesed, loving devotion. The refrain says five times that it endures forever (verses 1 to 4 and 29). The psalm's whole story, of rescue from death and entry into worship, is told as evidence of this steadfast love.

christ: Along with Psalm 110, few psalms matter more for the New Testament's portrait of Jesus. When Jesus entered Jerusalem, the crowds shouted hosanna and blessed him who comes in the name of the Lord, taking up verses 25 and 26 (Mark 11:9-10; John 12:13). Jesus himself quoted verses 22 and 23 after the parable of the tenants, naming himself as the rejected stone (Mark 12:10-11), and Peter used the same verse before the council to proclaim the crucified and risen Jesus (Acts 4:10-11; compare 1 Peter 2:7). Hebrews 13:6 quotes verse 6 as a word of confidence for believers. The pattern of the psalm, a righteous one pressed toward death, delivered, and brought into God's presence to the joy of the people, is the pattern the church found fulfilled in the death and resurrection of Jesus. As part of the Hallel, it was likely among the last songs Jesus sang before his arrest.

hard.q: The psalm speaks of cutting off the nations in the name of the LORD. How should readers understand its violent language?
hard.a: The speaker describes a defensive fight: he is surrounded, pushed to falling, and swarmed like bees, and his victory is credited entirely to God. Many scholars see a king's war behind it, in a world where every nation understood its battles as the acts of its god. The psalm's emphasis is not on the enemies' destruction but on the LORD's help to someone who would otherwise have died, and it closes in worship, not in triumph over the fallen. Christians have also read it in light of how the New Testament uses the psalm: the one who comes in the name of the Lord wins his victory by being rejected and raised, not by killing enemies, and his people are told to overcome evil with good (Romans 12:21). This does not erase the psalm's original setting, but it shows where its hope finally leads.

questions: The psalm says it is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in princes. What powerful people or institutions are you most tempted to rely on?
The stone the builders rejected became the cornerstone. Where have you seen God use what others dismissed?
Hosanna began as a cry for rescue and became praise. What prayer for help in your own life are you waiting to see become thanksgiving?
